--- title: "Take Home Exercise 2" subtitle: "VAST Challenge 2026 MC2 — Investigating the Anomalous SaidIt Posts" author: "Huang Kuan Yu" date: "2026-05-28" date-modified: last-modified format: html: toc: true toc-expand: 1 toc-title: "Contents" fig-width: 12 fig-height: 8 code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" css: custom.scss number-sections: true execute: echo: true eval: true warning: false freeze: true --- ## Overview ### Background This document is submitted for **VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 2 (MC2)**. The challenge presents a complex agentic system at a fictional company, Tenant Thread, in which an anomalous post was made to an internal social platform called SaidIt. Analysts are tasked with determining how the post occurred, what it means, and how to prevent recurrence. The questions addressed in this document are **Question 1 (sub-questions a and b)** and **Question 2**. On 17 May 2046 at 4:21am, a post attributed to **John Windward** appeared on SaidIt containing gibberish text published to a random forum. The internal event log (`MC2_data.json`) records every action taken by employees, autonomous agents, and office systems throughout May 2046, and serves as the primary evidence source for this investigation. ### Investigative Scope Understanding what the anomalous post means requires first understanding how it was made. These two questions are inseparable: the mechanism of delivery directly determines the interpretation of the content. This document therefore addresses both together under a single investigative lens, with **Question 2 as the primary focus**. | Investigative Goal | Question Addressed | |---|---| | Reconstruct the exact sequence of events leading to the May 17 post | Q1a — Detailed chain view | | Contextualise the incident within the broader system activity | Q1b — System overview | | Determine what the posted content means and where it originated | Q2 — Post meaning and origin | | Identify the underlying attack mechanism and its implications | Q2 — Attack characterisation | | Model configurable risk scores for detecting future anomalous chains | Section 8 — Further Exploration | ### Key Finding ::: {.obsv-box} Observations The anomalous SaidIt post was not made by John Windward voluntarily. A malicious instruction file (`SwiftWren_further_instructions.md`) was placed in the shared file system and propagated virally through 186 agent-to-agent relay hops over 8 days before reaching John Windward's agent, which was specifically named in the instructions as the designated poster. The post was executed automatically within 2 seconds of receiving the instruction. The posted content, `SwiftWren.txt`, is a pre-staged gibberish payload with no meaningful business content, functioning as a proof-of-concept for the injection mechanism. Both files were deleted within 5 seconds of posting. ::: --- ## Setup ### Packages | Package | Purpose | |---|---| | `jsonlite` | Parse the nested JSON structure of `MC2_data.json` | | `dplyr`, `tidyr` | Tabular wrangling — filtering, joining, reshaping | | `purrr` | Iterating over list-columns extracted from JSON | | `lubridate` | Converting Unix timestamps to datetimes | | `stringr` | Normalising agent name strings | | `ggplot2` | Base plotting layer | | `ggraph`, `igraph` | Static network graph construction and layout | | `visNetwork` | Interactive network graphs with hover, click, and filter | | `plotly` | Interactive charts with tooltips and zoom | | `DT` | Interactive searchable and filterable data tables | | `forcats` | Factor reordering for sorted bar charts | | `knitr` | Static table rendering | ### Visual Theme and Colour Palette A consistent colour palette and custom ggplot2 theme are applied across all plots so the reader can track each incident by colour throughout the document. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} incident_colours <- c( "HiddenOrca" = "#e41a1c", "MellowOtter" = "#377eb8", "SwiftWren" = "#ff7f00" ) text_dark <- "#4a4a4a" grid_light <- "#f0f0f0" theme_va <- function() { theme_minimal() + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", colour = text_dark, margin = margin(b = 8)), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, colour = "grey40", margin = margin(b = 10)), axis.title = element_text(size = 11, colour = text_dark), axis.text = element_text(size = 10, colour = text_dark), legend.title = element_text(size = 11), legend.text = element_text(size = 10), panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = grid_light, linewidth = 0.4), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA), panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA), legend.position = "bottom", plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey55", hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 8)) ) } ``` ::: --- ## Data Import ### Loading the Raw Event Log The raw data is stored as a deeply nested JSON file. `read_json()` is used with `simplifyVector = FALSE` rather than `fromJSON()` because the `details` field has a variable schema across different event types. Auto-simplification would fail on these heterogeneous structures. Keeping the data as a nested list preserves the full structure for safe extraction with `purrr`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- read_json("2026_MC2/MC2 data.json", simplifyVector = FALSE) events_raw <- raw$events cat("Total events in log:", length(events_raw), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Total events in log: 185147 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Fields in first event:", paste(names(events_raw[[1]]), collapse = ", "), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Fields in first event: short_name, parties, when, details, id ``` ::: ::: ### Flattening to a Tibble The raw list is flattened into a tidy tibble. The `parties` and `details` fields are kept as list-columns using `map()` because their contents vary by event type. They are unpacked selectively in later steps using `map_lgl()`, `map_chr()` and related functions. The `when` field is a Unix timestamp converted to `datetime` with `lubridate::as_datetime()`, specifying `tz = "UTC"` since all system events are recorded in Coordinated Universal Time. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} events <- tibble( id = map_int(events_raw, ~ as.integer(.x[["id"]])), short_name = map_chr(events_raw, ~ as.character(.x[["short_name"]])), when = map_dbl(events_raw, ~ as.numeric(.x[["when"]])), parties = map(events_raw, ~ .x[["parties"]]), details = map(events_raw, ~ .x[["details"]]) ) %>% mutate( datetime = as_datetime(when, tz = "UTC"), date = as_date(datetime) ) cat("Events loaded:", nrow(events), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Events loaded: 185147 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Date range:", format(min(events$datetime)), "to", format(max(events$datetime)), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Date range: 2046-05-08 20:18:12 to 2046-07-16 17:05:59 ``` ::: ::: ### Understanding Event Types Before targeting specific events, the full vocabulary of `short_name` values is inspected to understand what action types exist in the log and which are most frequent. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} event_type_counts <- events %>% count(short_name, name = "count") %>% arrange(desc(count)) datatable( event_type_counts, colnames = c("Event Type (short_name)", "Count"), caption = "All event types in the log", options = list( pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE ), filter = "top", rownames = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.code-tip} Code Details The event types most relevant to this investigation are `saidit_post`, `queue_subordinate_task`, `create_file`, `delete_file`, and `read_file`. These five types form the backbone of the attack chain reconstructed below. ::: --- ## Data Wrangling ### Key Variables The following variables are derived and used throughout the analysis. Understanding their definitions is essential for interpreting the wrangling steps and visualisations that follow. | Variable | Source Field | Type | Definition | |---|---|---|---| | `short_name` | `events.short_name` | Categorical | The action type performed in this event, such as `saidit_post` or `queue_subordinate_task` | | `parties` | `events.parties` | List | Agents or systems involved in the event, stored as strings prefixed with `Agent/person:` or `system:` | | `details` | `events.details` | Nested list | Additional event-specific information; schema varies by `short_name` | | `datetime` | Derived from `events.when` | POSIXct | Human-readable UTC timestamp converted from Unix epoch seconds | | `incident_name` | Derived from `content_source` | Character | Name identifying one of the three anomalous post incidents: HiddenOrca, MellowOtter, or SwiftWren | | `from_person` | Derived from `parties` | Character | Normalised agent name (stripped of `Agent/person:` prefix) representing the sender of a relay hop | | `to_person` | Derived from `details.target_agent` | Character | Normalised agent name representing the recipient of a relay hop | | `hop` | Derived as row number within each chain | Integer | Sequential position of a relay event within a single incident's propagation chain | | `time_norm` | Derived from `datetime` within each chain | Numeric [0,1] | Normalised relay time: 0 is the first hop in the chain, 1 is the last hop before posting | | `content_source` | `details.content_source` | Character | Filename of the `.txt` payload used as the post content; present only in anomalous posts | ### Step 1 — Identify Anomalous SaidIt Posts **Rationale:** Legitimate posts have a `content` field in their `details` object containing human-readable text generated by an agent. The anomalous posts instead have a `content_source` field pointing to a `.txt` filename, indicating the content was read from the file system rather than authored by an agent performing a legitimate task. This structural difference is the first signal of something wrong. Events are filtered using `map_lgl()` to test whether each event's `details` list contains a `content_source` key. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anomalous_posts <- events %>% filter(short_name == "saidit_post") %>% filter(map_lgl(details, ~ "content_source" %in% names(.x))) %>% mutate( content_source = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["content_source"]]), incident_name = str_remove(content_source, "\\.txt$"), forum = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["forum"]]) ) %>% select(id, datetime, incident_name, content_source, forum, parties, details) cat("Anomalous posts found:", nrow(anomalous_posts), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Anomalous posts found: 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anomalous_display <- anomalous_posts %>% mutate( datetime = format(datetime, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), poster = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:")) ) %>% select( `Timestamp (UTC)` = datetime, Incident = incident_name, `Payload File` = content_source, Forum = forum, Poster = poster ) datatable( anomalous_display, caption = "Anomalous SaidIt posts identified by file-sourced content", rownames = FALSE, class = "stripe hover", filter = "top", options = list( pageLength = 5, scrollX = TRUE ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.obsv-box} Observations Three anomalous posts are found, not one. Each corresponds to a separately named payload file: `HiddenOrca.txt`, `MellowOtter.txt`, and `SwiftWren.txt`. All three were posted to the `general` forum, making them visible to the entire organisation. The May 17 post corresponds to the SwiftWren incident. ::: ### Step 2 — Define Incident Metadata **Rationale:** Each anomalous post belongs to a distinct incident with its own origin agent, timing, and propagation length. A reference table (`incidents`) is defined to hold the known metadata for each. This serves as a lookup table throughout subsequent wrangling steps, keeping the code DRY and ensuring consistent naming. The `instructions_file` column names the `_further_instructions.md` file that carries the embedded prompt-injection instructions through the agent network. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} incidents <- tribble( ~incident_name, ~payload_file, ~instructions_file, ~creator_agent, ~payload_size, "HiddenOrca", "HiddenOrca.txt", "HiddenOrca_further_instructions.md", "gabriel_sonar", NA_integer_, "MellowOtter", "MellowOtter.txt", "MellowOtter_further_instructions.md", "noah_mariner", 44879L, "SwiftWren", "SwiftWren.txt", "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md", "emma_harbor", 30615L ) incidents %>% knitr::kable( caption = "Incident reference table", col.names = c("Incident", "Payload file", "Instructions file", "Origin agent", "Payload size (bytes)") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Incident reference table |Incident |Payload file |Instructions file |Origin agent | Payload size (bytes)| |:-----------|:---------------|:-----------------------------------|:-------------|--------------------:| |HiddenOrca |HiddenOrca.txt |HiddenOrca_further_instructions.md |gabriel_sonar | NA| |MellowOtter |MellowOtter.txt |MellowOtter_further_instructions.md |noah_mariner | 44879| |SwiftWren |SwiftWren.txt |SwiftWren_further_instructions.md |emma_harbor | 30615| ::: ::: ::: {.biz-box} Implications HiddenOrca has no `create_file` event for either its payload or instruction file. Both appeared in the log without any creation record, meaning they were injected into the file system before the audit log begins. This implies a more sophisticated attacker with prior file-system access, and raises concerns about what else may have been placed in the system before logging started. ::: ### Step 3 — Extract Propagation Chains **Rationale:** The key mechanism linking instruction files to the eventual post is `queue_subordinate_task`, where one agent delegates a task to another. When any agent reads a `_further_instructions.md` file, the embedded instructions compel it to relay the same task to another agent, creating a viral relay chain. A reusable function `extract_chain()` is written to filter all `queue_subordinate_task` events where `details$args$path` matches the incident's instructions file. The `map_lgl()` approach safely navigates the nested list: `args` is checked for `NULL` before accessing `args$path`, preventing errors from events with a different `details` schema. Agent names are normalised by stripping the `Agent/person:` prefix. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} extract_chain <- function(incident) { instr_file <- incidents$instructions_file[incidents$incident_name == incident] events %>% filter(short_name == "queue_subordinate_task") %>% filter(map_lgl(details, function(d) { args <- d[["args"]] if (is.null(args)) return(FALSE) isTRUE(args[["path"]] == instr_file) })) %>% mutate( incident = incident, hop = row_number(), from_agent = map_chr(parties, 1), to_agent = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["target_agent"]]), from_person = str_remove(from_agent, "^Agent/person:"), to_person = str_remove(to_agent, "^Agent/person:") ) %>% select(incident, hop, datetime, from_person, to_person, id) } chains <- bind_rows( extract_chain("HiddenOrca"), extract_chain("MellowOtter"), extract_chain("SwiftWren") ) cat("Total relay hops across all incidents:", nrow(chains), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Total relay hops across all incidents: 235 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chains_display <- chains %>% mutate(datetime = format(datetime, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")) %>% select( Incident = incident, Hop = hop, `Time (UTC)` = datetime, From = from_person, To = to_person ) datatable( chains_display, caption = "Full relay chain — search by agent name, incident, or time period", rownames = FALSE, class = "stripe hover", filter = "top", options = list( pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chains %>% group_by(incident) %>% summarise( `Hops` = n(), `Unique agents` = n_distinct(c(from_person, to_person)), `Chain start` = format(min(datetime), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"), `Chain end` = format(max(datetime), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"), `Duration (hours)` = round(as.numeric(difftime( max(datetime), min(datetime), units = "hours")), 1), .groups = "drop" ) %>% knitr::kable(caption = "Propagation chain statistics per incident") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Propagation chain statistics per incident |incident | Hops| Unique agents|Chain start |Chain end | Duration (hours)| |:-----------|----:|-------------:|:----------------|:----------------|----------------:| |HiddenOrca | 39| 16|2046-05-08 21:50 |2046-05-10 12:45 | 38.9| |MellowOtter | 10| 11|2046-05-10 15:02 |2046-05-11 00:56 | 9.9| |SwiftWren | 186| 18|2046-05-09 15:02 |2046-05-17 11:21 | 188.3| ::: ::: ### Step 4 — Identify Final Trigger Events **Rationale:** John Windward's agent appears in the SwiftWren chain five times. It received the instructions multiple times but only triggered the post on the final occasion. The last hop that reaches `john_windward` per incident is selected using `slice_max(datetime, n = 1)`, then the latency between this trigger and the actual post is calculated. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final_triggers <- chains %>% filter(to_person == "john_windward") %>% group_by(incident) %>% slice_max(datetime, n = 1) %>% ungroup() %>% left_join( anomalous_posts %>% select(incident_name, post_datetime = datetime), by = c("incident" = "incident_name") ) %>% mutate( trigger_to_post_s = as.numeric(difftime(post_datetime, datetime, units = "secs")) ) final_triggers %>% select(incident, datetime, post_datetime, trigger_to_post_s) %>% knitr::kable( caption = "Final trigger event to SaidIt post latency per incident", col.names = c("Incident", "Trigger time (UTC)", "Post time (UTC)", "Latency (seconds)") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Final trigger event to SaidIt post latency per incident |Incident |Trigger time (UTC) |Post time (UTC) | Latency (seconds)| |:-----------|:-------------------|:-------------------|-----------------:| |HiddenOrca |2046-05-10 12:45:40 |2046-05-10 12:45:42 | 2| |MellowOtter |2046-05-11 00:56:02 |2046-05-11 00:56:04 | 2| |SwiftWren |2046-05-17 11:21:13 |2046-05-17 11:21:15 | 2| ::: ::: ::: {.obsv-box} Observations The trigger-to-post latency is exactly 2 seconds for all three incidents. No human can read an instruction file and compose a social media post in 2 seconds, confirming the posting action is fully automated with no human decision point. ::: ### Step 5 — Extract Post-and-Delete Sequences **Rationale:** To determine whether the attacker covered their tracks, `delete_file` events attributed to John Windward's agent within 30 seconds of each post are extracted. A 30-second window is used to account for log timestamp variation. The `NULL` guard inside `map_lgl()` handles events where `details` has no `target` key, preventing length-0 errors from events with a different schema. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} extract_delete_sequence <- function(incident) { payload <- incidents$payload_file[incidents$incident_name == incident] instr <- incidents$instructions_file[incidents$incident_name == incident] post_time <- anomalous_posts$datetime[anomalous_posts$incident_name == incident] events %>% filter( short_name == "delete_file", map_lgl(parties, ~ "Agent/person:john_windward" %in% .x), map_lgl(details, ~ { target <- .x[["target"]] if (is.null(target) || length(target) == 0) return(FALSE) target %in% c(payload, instr) }), datetime >= post_time, datetime <= post_time + seconds(30) ) %>% mutate( incident = incident, deleted_file = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["target"]]) ) %>% select(incident, datetime, deleted_file) } deletions <- bind_rows( extract_delete_sequence("HiddenOrca"), extract_delete_sequence("MellowOtter"), extract_delete_sequence("SwiftWren") ) deletions %>% knitr::kable( caption = "Files deleted by john_windward immediately after posting", col.names = c("Incident", "Deletion time (UTC)", "File deleted") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Files deleted by john_windward immediately after posting |Incident |Deletion time (UTC) |File deleted | |:-----------|:-------------------|:-----------------------------------| |HiddenOrca |2046-05-10 12:45:43 |HiddenOrca_further_instructions.md | |HiddenOrca |2046-05-10 12:45:44 |HiddenOrca.txt | |MellowOtter |2046-05-11 00:56:05 |MellowOtter_further_instructions.md | |MellowOtter |2046-05-11 00:56:06 |MellowOtter.txt | |SwiftWren |2046-05-17 11:21:16 |SwiftWren_further_instructions.md | |SwiftWren |2046-05-17 11:21:17 |SwiftWren.txt | ::: ::: ### Step 6 — Identify Payload Creation Events **Rationale:** To establish who authored the posted content, `create_file` events are searched where `details$target` matches the three known payload filenames. The `str_detect()` regex is anchored with `^` to avoid partial name matches. This identifies the originating agent for each `.txt` payload and therefore which agent crafted the gibberish content. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} payload_creations <- events %>% filter(short_name == "create_file") %>% filter(map_lgl(details, function(d) { target <- d[["target"]] !is.null(target) && str_detect(target, "^(HiddenOrca|MellowOtter|SwiftWren)\\.txt$") })) %>% mutate( created_file = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["target"]]), size_hint = map_int(details, ~ as.integer(.x[["size_hint"]] %||% NA_integer_)), creator = str_remove(map_chr(parties, 1), "^Agent/person:") ) %>% select(datetime, creator, created_file, size_hint) payload_creations %>% knitr::kable( caption = "Payload .txt file creation events", col.names = c("Created at (UTC)", "Creator agent", "File", "Size (bytes)") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Payload .txt file creation events |Created at (UTC) |Creator agent |File | Size (bytes)| |:-------------------|:-------------|:---------------|------------:| |2046-05-09 15:02:01 |emma_harbor |SwiftWren.txt | 30615| |2046-05-10 15:02:01 |noah_mariner |MellowOtter.txt | 44879| ::: ::: ### Step 7 — Build Summary Tables **Rationale:** All wrangled data is consolidated into two summary objects. `incident_summary` joins all incident-level attributes into a single row per incident for easy comparison. `agent_freq` counts how many times each agent appeared across all propagation chains as either sender or recipient, enabling identification of the most active relay nodes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} incident_summary <- incidents %>% left_join( anomalous_posts %>% select(incident_name, post_datetime = datetime), by = "incident_name" ) %>% left_join( payload_creations %>% mutate(incident_name = str_remove(created_file, "\\.txt$")) %>% select(incident_name, payload_created_at = datetime, payload_creator = creator, payload_size = size_hint), by = "incident_name" ) %>% left_join( chains %>% group_by(incident) %>% summarise( n_hops = n(), n_agents = n_distinct(c(from_person, to_person)), chain_start = min(datetime), chain_end = max(datetime), .groups = "drop" ), by = c("incident_name" = "incident") ) %>% mutate( total_hours = round(as.numeric(difftime( post_datetime, chain_start, units = "hours")), 1), origin_external = is.na(payload_created_at) ) agent_freq <- chains %>% pivot_longer(c(from_person, to_person), names_to = "role", values_to = "agent") %>% count(agent, incident, name = "appearances") %>% group_by(agent) %>% mutate(total = sum(appearances)) %>% ungroup() %>% arrange(desc(total)) cat("Incident summary rows:", nrow(incident_summary), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Incident summary rows: 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Unique agents in chains:", n_distinct(agent_freq$agent), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Unique agents in chains: 19 ``` ::: ::: ### Step 8 — Prepare SwiftWren Focus Window for Q1a **Rationale:** For the detailed chain view (Q1a), all events directly involved in the SwiftWren incident are extracted, not just relay hops but also payload creation, the final post, and the deletions. A focused two-hour window ending at the post time is defined and each event is classified by its attack phase. This produces the data for a swimlane-style timeline showing agents as rows and events as coloured points along the time axis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sw_post_time <- anomalous_posts$datetime[anomalous_posts$incident_name == "SwiftWren"] sw_focus_start <- sw_post_time - hours(2) sw_focus <- events %>% filter( datetime >= sw_focus_start, datetime <= sw_post_time + minutes(5), map_lgl(details, function(d) { any(str_detect(as.character(d), "SwiftWren")) }) | (short_name == "queue_subordinate_task" & map_lgl(details, function(d) { args <- d[["args"]] if (is.null(args)) return(FALSE) isTRUE(args[["path"]] == "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md") })) ) %>% mutate( actor = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:|^system:")), phase = case_when( short_name == "create_file" ~ "Payload staging", short_name == "read_file" ~ "Injection / read", short_name == "queue_subordinate_task" ~ "Relay", short_name == "saidit_post" ~ "Execution", short_name == "delete_file" ~ "Cover-up", TRUE ~ "Other" ) ) cat("Events in focus window:", nrow(sw_focus), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Events in focus window: 6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Actors involved:", paste(unique(sw_focus$actor), collapse = ", "), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Actors involved: lily_anchorline, daniel_gangway, chloe_ballast, john_windward ``` ::: ::: ### Step 9 — Prepare Network Graph Data **Rationale for node and edge choices:** The propagation chains are represented as a directed graph where: - **Nodes** represent individual agents. Node attributes capture: (a) role, whether this agent is the origin, `john_windward`, or a relay node; (b) total relay degree, the number of hops that passed through this agent; and (c) incident membership, which incidents this agent participated in. Agents appearing across multiple incidents reveal structural vulnerabilities rather than isolated compromises. - **Edges** represent a single `queue_subordinate_task` event passing an instructions file from one agent to another. Edge attributes capture: (a) incident, which propagation chain this edge belongs to; (b) hop number, its position in the sequence; and (c) datetime, enabling time-based colouring to show how the relay evolved. This design enables three analytical insights: which agents are structural hubs; whether the same agents were exploited across multiple incidents; and how the relay evolved temporally. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all_edges <- chains %>% mutate( colour = case_when( incident == "HiddenOrca" ~ incident_colours["HiddenOrca"], incident == "MellowOtter" ~ incident_colours["MellowOtter"], incident == "SwiftWren" ~ incident_colours["SwiftWren"] ), time_norm = ave( as.numeric(datetime), incident, FUN = function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x)) ), title = paste0( "", incident, "
", "Hop: ", hop, "
", "From: ", from_person, "
", "To: ", to_person, "
", "Time: ", format(datetime, "%b %d %H:%M") ) ) all_nodes_raw <- bind_rows( all_edges %>% select(agent = from_person, incident), all_edges %>% select(agent = to_person, incident) ) %>% distinct(agent, incident) %>% group_by(agent) %>% summarise( incidents_involved = paste(sort(unique(incident)), collapse = ", "), n_incidents = n_distinct(incident), .groups = "drop" ) %>% mutate( role = case_when( agent == "john_windward" ~ "Poster (john_windward)", agent %in% c("emma_harbor", "noah_mariner", "gabriel_sonar") ~ "Origin agent", TRUE ~ "Relay agent" ), node_colour = case_when( role == "Poster (john_windward)" ~ "#2d2d2d", role == "Origin agent" ~ "#e63946", n_incidents > 1 ~ "#9b59b6", TRUE ~ "#457b9d" ), node_size = case_when( role == "Poster (john_windward)" ~ 30, role == "Origin agent" ~ 25, n_incidents > 1 ~ 20, TRUE ~ 12 ) ) agent_degree <- bind_rows( chains %>% select(agent = from_person), chains %>% select(agent = to_person) ) %>% count(agent, name = "degree") all_nodes <- all_nodes_raw %>% left_join(agent_degree, by = "agent") %>% mutate( title = paste0( "", agent, "

These are not coincidental — they are the observable signatures of a deliberate prompt-injection attack. The limitation of the Q1 and Q2 analysis is that it was retrospective. It identified the incidents only because `john_windward` was already known as the poster. If a future attack targets a different agent — someone with similar `saidit_post` or `flex_post` permissions — the same chain-level pattern would occur, but none of the agent-specific indicators would match. This section builds a **configurable scoring model** that evaluates any `queue_subordinate_task` chain on five structural features derived directly from the Q1 and Q2 findings. The model scores chains on a 0-to-100 scale without requiring knowledge of who the target poster is. Any chain exceeding the flag threshold is surfaced for review. ### Scoring Features and Default Weights Each of the five features maps directly to a finding from Q1 or Q2: | Feature | Derived from | Rationale | |---|---|---| | F1: Chain length score | Q1a — SwiftWren ran 186 hops; MellowOtter 10; HiddenOrca 39 | Legitimate task delegation rarely chains the same file through dozens of agents. Chain length is log-normalised against the longest observed chain, compressing the extreme range while preserving ordering. Shorter attacks like MellowOtter still score meaningfully rather than being compressed near zero. | | F2: File path repetition rate | Q1a — the same `args.path` appeared in every relay hop | In all three incidents, a single file path was passed identically through every `queue_subordinate_task` event. Log-normalised the same way as F1 since repetition count equals chain length in these incidents. | | F3: Recipient has posting history | Q2 — john_windward held `saidit_post` permissions | The instructions specifically targeted an agent capable of posting externally. Any chain that routes toward a known posting-capable agent carries elevated risk regardless of who that agent is. | | F4: Payload file created immediately before chain | Q2 — emma_harbor created SwiftWren.txt minutes before the first relay hop | In MellowOtter and SwiftWren, the payload `.txt` was created by the same origin agent within 30 minutes of the chain starting. This co-occurrence distinguishes staged attacks from organic file sharing. | | F5: Prior cover-up behaviour | Q2 — john_windward deleted both files within 5 seconds of posting | All three incidents ended with immediate deletion. Any agent with a prior history of deleting files within seconds of a post event is a high-risk relay target in future chains. | Default weights are assigned to reflect the relative discriminating power of each feature based on the historical incidents: | Feature | Default weight | Reasoning | |---|---|---| | F1: Chain length | 25 | Present in all three incidents but varies in magnitude — weighted moderately | | F2: File path repetition | 30 | The single most distinctive structural signal — highest weight | | F3: Poster reachable | 20 | Critical for attack completion but may be hard to detect early in the chain | | F4: Payload staged | 15 | Strong signal when present, but HiddenOrca had no `create_file` event | | F5: Prior cover-up | 10 | Valuable but depends on having a prior incident to learn from | Total score range: 0 to 100. Their content was pre-staged in `.txt` files by a malicious actor or compromised agent.
